REJB 1998-06139 - Texte
intégral

CITATION: B.-C. (T.) v. D. F. (J.B.)

Cour
supérieure
(Chambre de la famille)

CANADA

PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC

DISTRICT DE Montréal

NO : 500-04-000232-950

500-14-000099-952

DATE :  1998-04-22

EN PRÉSENCE DE :

Jeannine M.
Rousseau , J.C.S.

B.-C. (T.)

Applicant

v.

D. F. (J.B.)

Respondent

et

B. (T.), B. (C.), T.-B. (N.) and B. (J.)

Mis en cause

D.F. (J.B.)

Applicant

v.

The Public Curator of Quebec

Mis en cause

Rousseau:-

The Litigation

1
The Court is seized with
applications concerning the custody and tutorship of J.B., who is 111/2 years
old.

2
His mother died when he
was born; his father died when he was 81/2 years old.

3
J. has been the object of
substantial litigation, even before his father died, both in Quebec and in
British Columbia, where his maternal grand-mother and his step-grandfather
reside.

4
The adults involved in
this custody-tutorship dispute are the following:

J. paternal aunt, T.B., and her
husband M.C.;

J. maternal grand-mother and
step-grandfather, N.T.-B. and C.B.;

C.F., the executrix of the will
of J.B., J. father, which will also appointed her tutrix to the child.

The Law

5
The principles are simple
and clear:

Section 32

Civil Code of Quebec

Every child has a right to the
protection, security and attention that his parents or the persons acting in
their stead are able to give to him.

Section 33 C.C.Q.

Every decision concerning a child
shall be taken in light of the child's interests and the respect of his rights.

Consideration is given, in
addition to the moral, intellectual, emotional and material needs of the child,
to the child's age, health, personality and family environment, and to the
other aspects of his situation.

The Trial

6
This case was heard on
June 25, 26 and 27, 1997; it was continued on July 22 and 23, 1997 so that N.
and C.B. could attend and testify; pleadings were done in writing, and included
written submissions from Ian W. Caldwell, barrister and solicitor, acting on
behalf of J. pursuant to an appointment under the
Family Relations Act of
British Columbia
; his 11-page report is filed as exhibit I-7.

7
Fourteen persons
testified in person, including one expert witness; the affidavit of one other
person, B.K., was accepted in lieu of her attendance before the Court.

8
The most important
testimony was that of the members of the two sets of families: T.B.-C., M.C.
and T.B., N.T.-B. and C.B.

9
The testimony of D.F.
provided an understanding of the background to the dispute and of the varying,
overlapping and evolving relationship between J.B., J. father, and the members
of his own family (mother, sister and brother-in-law), the members of his
wife's family (sister, mother and step-father), and with her.

10
Mtre Caroline Polak, who
had acted previously for Mrs B.-C., and Mtre Eva Petras, who had acted
previously for the child, added some information.

11
Friends and neighbours
of T.B. and of the B.C., (V.S.L., J.R.L., M.H., H.W., B.K., Z.K.) testified as
to the grand-mother's, the aunt's and the uncle's relationship with J. and
other members of the family, and as to their personal qualities as parents,
teachers and individuals.

12
Dominic A. D'Abate
testified as an expert; his testimony is discussed below.

The End Result

13
After the first three
days, the Court was not convinced that it was in the child's interest to return
to live with his aunt T. in Montreal; in other words, petitioner B.-C. had not
discharged her burden of proof;

14
nothing in the evidence
presented during the last two days changed that conclusion; to the contrary, it
was strengthened;

15
moreover, the last two
days' evidence convinced the Court that J. should remain with his B.
grand-parents and that custody should be entrusted to them.

T.B.-C. and M.C.

16
The Court has come to
the conclusion, on the basis of the evidence put before it, that Mrs B.-C. is
not credible and that her “custodial” capacity is insufficient.

17
As to M.C., he supports
his wife, T.B.; and, as in his wife's version of things, there are gaps and
questions which remain unanswered.

Credibility

18
The essence of T.B.-C.
position is that she was obliged to leave J. in British Columbia and that she
was then cut off from him by the B.

19
In itself, it was not a
persuasive story and, as discussed below, when the Court heard the version of
Mr and Mrs B., it realized how blatantly false Mrs B.-C. story was.

20
The Court grants her no
credibility.

Custodial Capacity

21
Mrs B.-C.
presented herself to the Court as the only mother J. ever knew: he bonded to
her; it was to her home that he was brought at 31/2 weeks of age when the
father could not take care of him; she and her husband took care of him with
the help of her own mother, T.B.; J. called her and her husband
“Mommy” and “Daddy”; their two daughters consider him
as their brother; she and her husband treated him as their son; she even went
to Court to gain legal custody of J. in 1989, against her own brother, J.
father; this litigation lasted until the December 1992 final judgment, which
cut her off from J.; she and her brother later reconciled and J. spent more and
more time with her and her family; it is in J. interest to live with her and
her family;

22
in
summary, this is what Mrs B.-C. put forth.

23
Most of
the above may be true, though there are large gaps in Mrs B.-C. presentation of
facts. However, what is worrisome is what has gone on since early 1995, even if
one accepts Mrs B.-C. version of J. being alienated from her and the other
members of the B. family by the B., (which version the Court does not accept).

24
The last
time she really saw J. was in January 1995, at the Vancouver Airport, when she
left to return to Montreal and J. stayed with the B., she had whisked him there
shortly before, without notice, hurriedly, to remove him from Quebec, so that
she would not have to hand him over to Miss F. under the terms of an order
issued by the Superior Court.

25
According
to Mrs B.-C., she was prevented by the B. from bringing J. back to Montreal;
she left him there nonetheless, as the B. were supposed to give J. back to her
in a few months;

26
she
testified however that the situation changed after she and her husband refused
to give $5,000 to the B., which the latter had requested for their legal fees;
according to her, they were subsequently cut off from telephone access to J.
during July and August 1995 and were lied to concerning the child's
whereabouts;

27
moreover,
the child had changed; he was rude and obnoxious and impolite over the phone;

28
the B.-C.
felt J. was being brain-washed and controlled; they felt their telephone
conversations were supervised and recorded;

29
and in the
spring of 1996, when the B.-C. flew out to British Columbia for a hearing on
the B. application, J. refused to talk to them at the Court house;

30
they have
not seen him since.

31
Let us now
examine the extent of the B.-C. efforts during this period of time, i.e.
February 1995 to June 1997, to remain in touch with J., the child they
testified they loved as their own son.

32
In
1995
,
there were phone calls, presents, one of which they had a hard time to get
accepted by the B., and cards drawn by their daughters; but there were no trips
to British Columbia, not even an attempted trip to British Columbia, to see J.:
if he was, in fact, being cut off from his B. family by his B. family and
prevented from staying in touch, would not a face-to-face visit be a normal
response? If, in fact, this adored nephew was being alienated from his Montreal
family, why let the situation go on? Why not go to where the problem was, i.e.
in British Columbia, and do something? See him, touch him, hug him, talk to
him, answer his questions! J., at that time, i.e. the summer of 1995, had just
turned nine; he was a little boy!

33
No
credible answer was provided to those queries; the purported threat of violence
by Mr B. was not sufficient justification; police protection could have been
requested.

34
In
1996
,
Mrs B.-C. and her husband flew to British Columbia to attend a hearing on the
B. application for custody; they did not take advantage of being there to get
in touch with J. Court-appointed lawyer, to consult with him, to get
information as to J. well-being, his needs, etc.; if, as they allege, J. was
being brain-washed, would it not have been normal to see what psychological
help or testing was available?

35
But they
did nothing.

36
They
stated that J. walked away from them and refused to have anything to do with
them; could they not have walked up to him, at least, and perhaps given him a
hug? Why put the onus on J.? Why put the burden on the child? Why not, as
adults, take an initiative themselves?

37
No
satisfactory answer was provided.

38
It is true
that Mrs B.-C. presented an application to the Quebec Superior Court to have J.
visit her and her family in Montreal for three weeks during the 1996 summer;
but it was served on the 26
th
of July and made presentable on the 1
st
of August; and the Court
refused her request for an interim order on that day.

39
Some comments
immediately come to mind: the 1
st
of August is very late to request a three week visit by a child who
attends school; and if the B.-C. really wanted to see J., why had they not done
something practical while in British Columbia some months before?

40
The Court
is well aware of the jurisdictional aspects of the dispute. But such legal
niceties would not have prevented the B.-C. from at least trying to do
something practical while they were in British Columbia; and they did nothing,
as discussed above.

41
Thus, the
Court gives little value or weight to the July 1996 application to see J.

42
As to
1997
,
they only got in touch with him on June 24, 1997, for his 11
th
birthday, the day
before the trial began; the previous phone call had been in December 1996, six
months before!

43
According
to Mrs B.-C., she stopped calling in December 1996 because the calls were
“too painful” for her... That is not a satisfactory answer; in
fact, it is a worrisome answer.

44
As to her
and her husband's plans for J. if they get custody, they explained they would
want J. to go back to the same school he had attended before and which their
two daughters are now attending;

45
according
to Mrs B.-C., if J. came back to Montreal, he would “become himself
again”.

46
This
simplistic assumption is unrealistic: according to their own evidence, J. has
been brainwashed, he no longer considers himself to be Jewish, he now wants to
be called “B.”, not “B.”, etc.

47
And just
bringing him back to live with them will solve everything? This makes no sense
and indicate a sad lack of custodial capacity.

Dominic A. D'Abate

48
Dominic A.
D'Abate testified as an expert witness on behalf of Mrs B.-C.

49
Mr D'Abate
is a social worker, with a Ph.D. in Social Services. His services had been
retained in the spring of 1996; his original report was issued in May of 1996
and supplemented by additional notes in May and June 1996; he met Mrs B.C., Mr
C., Mrs T.B., the two B.C. daughters; no testing was carried out;

50
he took
cognisance of various documents:

three detailed
affidavits signed by Mrs B.-C., Mr C. and Mrs B. in the spring of 1996;

some newspaper
articles;

some professional
reports:

by Susan Goldsmith,
psychologist, concerning the child, Jesse, whom she was seeing in British Columbia;
originally there were three reports (February and August 1995 and April 1996);
two more came later (July and December 1996);

by two Montreal
psychologists, whose services had been retained by Mrs B.-C. and by J.B., J.
father, in the 1989-1992 period, during the original custody litigation;

letters from J.;

51
he also
saw some other documents when he met with Mrs B.-C. then lawyer in the spring
of 1996, but he does not remember which; he stated he might also have had some
other documents in his file which he would have since given back, but he had no
specific recollection;

52
he had no
access to J., no to the B., the maternal grand-parents, with whom J. was
living.

53
Thus, all
his information came from the B.-C. group (grand-mother, aunt and uncle),
except for the psychologists' reports.

54
Mr D'Abate
stated he had tried to cross-check the information provided to him but that he
did not pursue the exercise as there were so many documents. He stated he
assumed that what he was being told was true.

55
This
approach surprises the Court greatly: surely a critical eye is required in
doing such assessments. Such an approach, i.e. cautious, would particularly be
required in a case such as this, where two previous experts, both
psychologists, had tested Mrs B.-C. and had expressed conflicting views.

56
Questioned
about the cautionary note concerning Mrs B.-C. in one of the reports he had
been given, Mr D'Abate recognised he was aware of it but that he did not give
it great weight; he pointed out that a complaint had been made against this
psychologist to the “Ordre des psychologistes du Québec” and
that the psychologist was found guilty; the decision of the Disciplinary
Committee was filed in the record and the appeal judgment provided subsequently.

57
Mr
D'Abate's answer is not responsive: true, complaints were laid against the
psychologist and true, the psychologist was found guilty — but not of
faulty testing. In fact, the complaints, the disciplinary decision and the
appeal decision had nothing to do with the validity or value of the tests
carried out on Mrs B.C. once she agreed to them
1
.

58
Thus the
Court must conclude that Mr D'Abate's report is based on facts coming from one
sole source, the B.C. family, which facts were not examined with a cautious
eye, notwithstanding the strong indication of possible lying by Mrs B.C.

59
Mr D'Abate
concludes to the alienation of J. by the B. grand-parents from B.C. family.

60
The Court
cannot accept that conclusion as solid and convincing:

1. it is based on
facts, many of which came from the B.C. family and were accepted uncritically;
the Court grants no credibility to Mrs B.-C., as explained above; thus any
conclusion based on unverified facts provided by Mrs B.-C. is of minimal value;

2. but even
assuming those facts were true, there is another possibility, which the Court
suggested to Mr D'Abate, i.e. that of J. seeing himself abandoned by his
Montreal family and thus having to rely on his B. family: for him, it would be
a matter of survival to cling to the E; and there would be no need for
alienation by the B.

61
This
dispute seems to have given raise to an inordinate number of complaints, all by
Mrs B.-C. or Mr C.

to the “Ordre
des psychologues du Québec” concerning the psychologist mentioned
above;

to the Bar of
Quebec concerning the fees and services of one of her previous lawyers;

to the Bar of
Quebec concerning another lawyer (unidentified) in either this dispute or the
previous one;

to the College of Psychologists
of British Columbia concerning psychologist Susan Goldsmith.

Thea Boness

62
T.B., J.
paternal grand-mother, is a very strong willed person; she has shown she can be
ruthless: see,
inter alia
, her November 17, 1989 and January 26, 1990
affidavits (exhibits I-1 and I-2) in a previous file, when her two children, T.
and J., were battling over the custody of J.

63
Mrs B. was
originally on T. side in 1989 and then switched to J. side, against T.; she
then swore her daughter was a liar, a cheat, prone to hysterics, afflicted with
drug dependency and behavioural problems and required psychological or
psychiatric help;

64
when
confronted with those statements in the present case, where she is now
supporting T., she brushed the contradictions aside; in a February 1995
affidavit (I-3), she swore that she had sided with her son because she thought
he had cleaned up his life and that J. should learn to know and love his
father; nothing is said therein about T. “previous” problems;

65
she
answered questions with questions; she ignores those facts which do not suit
her and clings to her own view of things; she twists facts to suit her: compare
paragraph 20 of her November 17, 1989 affidavit (I-1), paragraph 20 of her
January 26, 1990 affidavit (1-2) and the August 18, 1997 letter from Mrs B.C.
and Mrs T. a B. lawyer;

66
she even
stated that she was forced to sign an affidavit; the idea of T.B. being
“forced” to sign anything is preposterous: she is strong and
ruthless.

67
In
summary, the testimony of T.B. provides insight as to how the situation got as
messy as it did, but little more.

N.T.-B. and C.B.

68
The
testimony of N.T.-B. and of C.B. allowed the Court to get an overall picture of
the situation and to arrive at a realistic evaluation of what had happened.

69
In
particular, Mrs B.-C. version of J., remaining in British Columbia in January
1995 made no sense; according to her, she was prevented by the B. from
returning to Montreal with J., as she had been ordered to by the Superior Court
judgment; after her testimony, the Court had asked some questions and had
expressed scepticism that a grown woman, left by herself in the B. apartment
with J., could not simply have walked out and, if need be, gone to the police,
specially as she was under a Court order to bring the child back to Montreal;
no satisfactory answer was provided by Mrs B.-C.

70
However,
when Mr and Mrs B. testified, their version of J. arriving in British Columbia
and of his staying there answered those unanswered questions. The pieces of the
puzzle fell into place.

71
The B.
testimony was clear and credible; they did not shy away from issues; they
explained how they changed their mind concerning D.F. and how their
relationship with the B. family evolved.

72
Contrary
to the B.C., they have shown, through their actions, in a continuous fashion,
on a day to day basis, that they care deeply for J., that they love him, and
that they can take care of him;

73
both Mr
and Mrs B. testified as to how J. was when he arrived in January 1995, what
they did for him, how he changed and evolved and how he is now; they have seen
to his needs: intellectual, religious, emotional and physical;

74
they have
plans to move to Vancouver Island, to be close to their other daughter and her
family, i.e. J. aunt and cousins.

75
As to the
June 20, 1990 incident (see exhibit R-28), involving T.B. and C.B., it was most
unfortunate, from beginning to end, i.e. the pressing of charges against Mr B.
by Mrs B.

76
and after
having heard Mrs B. testify and taken cognisance of her ruthlessness and
tendency to see things only her way, or in a way that suits her, the Court
gives credence to Mr B. version.

The Telephone Conversations

77
Mrs B.-C.
filed as exhibits a series of tape recordings of telephone conversations; these
recordings were part of the material of which Mr D'Abate took cognisance.

78
These
recordings are very instructive.

79
Mrs B.-C.
and her husband knew they were being recorded; if T.B.-C. was on her best
behaviour during these recorded conversations, her worst behaviour must be
outrageous; Mrs B.-C. comes across as a complaining and frequently emotionally
bullying adult; she was aggressive, rude, intent on picking a fight with C.B.,
who finally responded in kind;

80
J. comes
across as a very nice child, very polite; there are no traces of the rude and
impolite manner of which Mrs B.-C. and Mrs B. complained before the Court;

81
Mr C.
comes across generally as a polite and mild mannered adult.

82
In
summary, the five days of hearing, including the substantial number of
exhibits, bring the Court to the conclusion that J. is well off with the B.,
and that it is in his interest to remain with them; T.B.-C. has not
demonstrated that it is in J. interest to be taken care of by her, far from it.

83
In
summary, the Court does not believe, nor trust, either T.B. or T.B.-C. and J.
must be protected from them.

Conclusions

The Court:

No. 500-04-000232-950:

84
GIVES ACT
of the declaration of D.F. that she no longer wishes to request the custody of
J.B. and, in consequence, DISMISSES the Motion for Custody presented by D.F.;

85
Without
costs;

86
DISMISSES
the Motion for custody presented by T.B.-C.;

87
Having
arrived at the conclusion that it is in the interest of J.B. that his custody
be granted to N.T.-B. and to C.B., and in light of their express declaration to
the Court that they wish to have J. remain with them and to be responsible for
him, GRANTS custody of J.B. to N.T.B. and to C.B.;

88
GRANTS to
D. F. access rights to J.B., the modalities of such access to be agreed upon
between D.F., N.T.-B. and C.B., taking into consideration the wishes of J.B.,
such access to include, as a minimum, written correspondence, monthly telephone
calls and a yearly visit in British Columbia;

89
GRANTS to
T.B., T.B.-C. and M.C. no access rights to J.B.

90
RECOMMENDS
that any future access be granted only if, as and when J.B. has psychological
help and support in that regard;

91
With costs
against T.B.-C. in favour of D.F., N.T.-B. and C.B.;

No. 500-14-000099-952:

92
CONFIRMS
the nomination of D.F. as tutrix to J.B., born on June 24, 1986, with
provisional execution notwithstanding appeal;

93
Without
costs.

Rousseau

Mtre Johanne Rhéaume-Lightner
, for D.F.

M
e
Julius Grey
, for T.B.-C.

Mtre Jean Barrière
, for C.B. et N.T.-B.

1.
The complaints against this psychologist,
one of those earlier involved in the file, concerned two letters written by him
to J.B. lawyer in April and November 1990, before having met T.B.C.

It was in March 1991 that he met and tested
both T.B.C. and M.C.; his conclusions concerning Mrs B.-C. are contained in his
April 1, 1991 report, of which Mr D'Abate acknowledge having taken cognisance.
